text: I think water has a calming effect on most people. The sound of waves or a river is repetitive in a pleasant way, and it helps the mind slow down after a busy week. There's probably an evolutionary reason too — for thousands of years, living near water meant food and safety. That may be why seaside flats are always so much more expensive.

text: It's quite serious in some regions. The Aral Sea is the most famous example — it shrank dramatically because too much water was taken for farming. Rivers near big industrial towns also suffer from waste from factories. The situation is slowly improving, but I think fines for companies should be much higher, otherwise it's cheaper for them to pollute than to clean up.

text: Definitely. Many city children today know more about animals from cartoons than from real life. Time outdoors improves their physical health, but it also teaches them things a classroom can't, like how to judge risks or how to entertain themselves without a screen. Schools could help by organising regular trips, because not every family has a car or the time to do it.

text: The simplest thing is not to leave rubbish behind, which sounds obvious but is still a huge problem at picnic spots. People can also use less plastic and fewer harsh chemicals at home, since a lot of that ends up in the water. And local volunteer clean-ups are surprisingly effective — they remove waste and make people much more aware of the problem.
